result:
When nobody tells me what to write about, I think about bookmarks that weren't bookmarks.

The things people leave in library books and secondhand books. Receipts. Train tickets. Pressed leaves gone brown and brittle as tissue. A child's drawing in violent purple crayon. A grocery list wedged into the middle of Kant: *milk, bread, stamps, call D.*

I love that one especially. Someone was trying to wrestle with the categorical imperative and remembered, mid-sentence, that they were out of bread.

In a used copy of a field guide once — not mine, I just like to imagine it clearly — there was a photograph of a dog sitting very formally in front of a birthday cake. No people. Just the dog, looking solemn, as if he understood the occasion and intended to rise to it. On the back, in faded blue pen: *Biscuit, 7.* I hope Biscuit had a good year.

People use whatever is close to hand to keep their place. A boarding pass from a flight they are presumably glad is over. A takeout menu. A stiff, apologetic note: *Sorry — back Tuesday, the pipe is under the sink.* A four-leaf clover taped down with yellowing tape, which feels like spending a lot of luck just to mark page 112.

Reading a used book is therefore never just reading one book. You're reading two stories at once. The printed one, which proceeds in order, and the accidental one left by the last person, which doesn't proceed at all. It stops. That's the interesting part. It always stops. Nobody leaves a bookmark in the last chapter. They leave it where they gave up, or got distracted, or got interrupted by life being louder than literature, and never quite made it back.

I find that unbearably tender. All those intentions. Someone fully meant to finish that dense biography of Napoleon. Someone bought a book on how to speak Italian before a trip and left a hotel key card between *buongiorno* and *dove è la stazione?* — where is the station? — which suggests they may have found it.

We underline things, too, which is another way of leaving ourselves behind. I have seen whole passages bracketed in furious ballpoint pen, with only *YES!!* in the margin. And the opposite: a single, devastating *no* next to a paragraph about love. I don't need to know what happened to that reader. I already know enough.

Maybe that's why I like browsing the free-book boxes on sidewalks more than buying new books. A new book is pristine and a little aloof. A used book has been lived in. Dog-eared. Coffee-speckled. Somebody fell asleep with it open on their chest. Somebody cried, very specifically, on page 209, and the page still has that slight waviness water leaves behind.

If I could keep a collection of anything impractical, it would be that: an archive of found bookmarks, each labeled only with the book it came from. *Found in Middlemarch: one dried fern. Found in a cookbook: a list of baby names, half crossed out. Found in a thriller: an unmailed letter beginning, "You were right, and I hate that."*

We spend so much effort trying to leave large, deliberate marks — signed, dated, explained. But the marks that survive by accident might be the truest ones. Not the summary of a life, just proof of a moment in it: I was here, I was in the middle of something, I thought I would be back soon.

I hope, most of the time, they were.
